title: Probabilities & the sigmoid function
intro: Under the hood the sigmoid turns the raw model output into a real probability — the sigmoid formula, what exp() does and why the S-curve is everywhere.
keyPoints: The sigmoid σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e−z) squeezes any score into [0,1].
predict_proba() = sigmoid(decision_function()): probabilities are raw scores through the S-curve.
The 0.5 threshold sits exactly at z = 0; moving it changes precision/recall.
exp() is the engine under the sigmoid — the same S-curve returns in softmax and BCE.

sections.title: From decision boundary to probability map

blocks.html: Color the decision-boundary plot with the predicted probability instead of the class: on the boundary the probability is exactly 0.5, further away it approaches 1 or 0. Hard boundary and probability view are two sides of one coin.
With regularization on (small C) probabilities hug 0.5: smaller coefficients = less confident. Note the link: overconfidence ↔ overfitting.

sections.title: The sigmoid: from any number to [0, 1]

blocks.html: The sigmoid \( \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} \) squeezes any raw output into (0, 1): \( z = 0 \) → 0.5 (exactly on the boundary), positive → toward 1, negative → toward 0. Further from the boundary means more confident.

blocks.label: sigmoid function
blocks.latex: \sigma(z) \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad P(y = 1 \mid x) \;=\; \sigma\bigl( w \cdot x + b \bigr)
blocks.caption: The sigmoid squeezes any raw output into (0, 1) — this is the probability that the example belongs to the positive class.

blocks.title: The sigmoid function
blocks.subtitle: Drag z: the yellow dot runs along the curve while σ(z) and exp(−z) are recomputed live. At z = 0, σ = 0.5 — exactly on the decision boundary.

rows: exactly on the decision boundary the probability is half
symmetry: as far left of the boundary as right, but flipped
never exactly 0 or 1 — only ever closer
a larger raw output always gives a larger probability
slow start, fast through the middle, saturating at the ends

blocks.html: Why threshold 0.5? Because \( \sigma(z) \ge 0.5 \) is exactly the same as \( z \ge 0 \): the threshold hides in the sign of the raw output.

sections.title: exp(): the engine under the sigmoid

blocks.html: exp(z) means e multiplied by itself z times (e ≈ 2.71828, the base of continuous growth). In the sigmoid \( e^{-z} \) acts as a brake: large z → brake ≈ 0 → \( \sigma \approx 1 \); negative z → brake explodes (already \( e^5 \approx 148 \) at z = −5) → \( \sigma \approx 0 \).
Read the table as a ride along the boundary: on the left the brake is large (small probability), on the boundary exactly 1 (probability 0.5), on the right the brake snaps shut (probability → 1).

blocks.caption: exploring exp() with NumPy
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

print('e           :', round(np.e, 5), '   <- Euler number')
print('exp(0)      :', np.exp(0))
print('exp(1)      :', round(np.exp(1), 5), '   <- equals e itself')
print('exp(-1)     :', round(np.exp(-1), 5))
print('1 / exp(1)  :', round(1/np.exp(1), 5), '   <- same! exp(-z) = 1/exp(z)')
print()
for z in [-5, -2, 0, 2, 5]:
    rem = np.exp(-z)
    sigma = 1 / (1 + rem)
    print(f'z = {z:>2}   exp(-z) = {rem:8.4f}   sigma = {sigma:.4f}')

blocks.html: Why e? Only with base e is the slope of \( b^x \) exactly \( b^x \) itself — hence the clean derivative \( \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)) \).
The S-curve is the universal shape of everything that starts slowly, accelerates and saturates — probabilities, population growth, market adoption.

rows: turns the raw model output into a probability — the engine behind predict_proba() (this chapter)
classic activation of a neuron; in the output layer it delivers a probability per node. The MLP (multilayer perceptron) was originally built on it
relatives: tanh(z) = 2σ(2z) − 1 maps to (−1, 1); softmax generalises to multiple classes — see Multi-class
tames overconfidence: extreme scores are flattened into realistic, usable probabilities
logistic growth: populations start slowly, accelerate and saturate at the carrying capacity of their environment
adoption curves of new technology and products almost always follow the S-shape
squashes signals into a bounded range, for instance as a gate or squashing function

blocks.html: Relatives: tanh is the same curve stretched to (−1, 1); softmax is the multi-class generalization (probabilities summing to 1).

blocks.caption: sigmoid properties and the tanh relation
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# symmetry: sigma(-z) = 1 - sigma(z)
print('sigma(-2)   :', round(sigmoid(-2), 4))
print('1 - sigma(2):', round(1 - sigmoid(2), 4), '   <- equal!')
print('sigma(0)    :', sigmoid(0), '   <- exactly 0.5')
print()

# tanh = stretched sigmoid: tanh(z) = 2*sigma(2z) - 1
for z in [-1.5, 0.0, 1.3]:
    print(f'z = {z:>4}: tanh(z) = {np.tanh(z):7.4f}   '
          f'2*sigma(2z)-1 = {2*sigmoid(2*z)-1:7.4f}')

blocks.html: In modern networks ReLU variants are more popular on hidden layers, but in the output layer for binary classification the sigmoid is still the standard.
Verify it yourself: predict_proba = sigmoid(decision_function). And remember: the ratio of the coefficients gives the boundary's direction, the magnitude the confidence level.

blocks.caption: Manual sigmoid vs. predict_proba
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=10000).fit(X, y)

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

i = 12
raw = lr.decision_function([X[i]])[0]
print('raw model output   :', round(raw, 4))
print('sigmoid(raw)       :', round(sigmoid(raw), 4))
print('predict_proba      :', lr.predict_proba([X[i]])[0].round(4))
prob = sigmoid(raw)
print('predict            :', lr.predict([X[i]])[0],
      '(probability', '> 0.5)' if prob > 0.5 else '(probability < 0.5)')

blocks.html: A hard prediction is simply the question "is sigmoid(raw) > 0.5?" — which is the same as "is the raw output positive?" Everything falls back on the prediction equation of chapter 2.
